chapter: Les Hite, Sebastian's and Duke Ellington
title: Duke's built-in replacement and the Hodges departure in 1951
summary: Duke counted on Royal as a substitute for alto players; when Hodges left in 1951 Royal had just joined Basie.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Tell me about that. You told me that because you had worked with Duke in the past, Duke knew that you could step right in and take over any part (inaudible) there and when Johnny Hodges left in '51, you said Duke called you, right?

Well, Johnny was always the very strong force of the Ellington Orchestra and by Johnny leaving, everyone thought that, 'Oh, gee, that's going to put a big hole in the orchestra,' so Duke always sort of held me as an ace in the hole or a card up his sleeve, because he would know that anytime he was in hailing distance of me, all he had to do was call and I'd come over and do the job for him, whether it was playing the lead chair or whether it was playing Johnny's chair or whatever it was. As long as it was alto, I could do the job.
So, when Johnny decided to go out on his own in early

'51, around the first of the year, I think Johnny left him in Las Vegas and he just knew everything was cool. Johnny could leave if he wanted to, because he was within 300 miles of Los Angeles and I was here. That time, he called and Count Basie had just beat him by a week and I was in New York with the Count Basie Group.

So, we always had a big laugh about that. But he ended up getting an excellent replacement, because instead of getting me, he got Willie Smith and Willie joined him in New York a little bit later after that, which Willie was one of the better players of all time. So, he didn't lose nothing anyway.
Yeah, when he was there, he was fine.
